title: 5.3 Connective Tissue Adaptations to Anaerobic Training

cards.front: What are osteoblasts, and how do they initiate the process of bone modeling in response to mechanical loading?
cards.back: Osteoblasts are specialized bone-forming cells that migrate to the outer bone surface (the periosteum) when stimulated by mechanical strain. They manufacture and secrete proteins—primarily collagen molecules—to build the bone matrix, which subsequently becomes mineralized with calcium phosphate crystals (hydroxyapatite) to increase bone diameter and structural strength.

cards.front: How do cortical bone and trabecular bone differ in structure and adaptive response rate to mechanical loading?
cards.back:
• Cortical (Compact) Bone: Dense, rigid outer shell of bone tissue with a low surface area-to-mass ratio that adapts relatively slowly to mechanical stress.
  • Trabecular (Spongy) Bone: Porous, delicate interlocking plates of bone with a high surface area-to-mass ratio that responds significantly more rapidly to adaptive mechanical strain.

cards.front: What is Minimal Essential Strain (MES), and what fraction of fracture force is required to trigger new bone formation?
cards.back: Minimal Essential Strain (MES) is the threshold stimulus of mechanical strain required to initiate new bone formation. It is estimated to be approximately 1/10 (10%) of the force required to fracture a bone. Forces exceeding MES signal osteoblasts to form new bone, while forces below MES do not stimulate bone modeling.

cards.front: What is the typical time course for measurable increases in bone mineral density (BMD), and how early do osteogenic adaptations begin at the cellular level?
cards.back: Measurable increases in BMD require a long time course—typically approximately 6 months or longer. However, cellular osteogenesis begins within the first few workouts, triggering the systemic secretion of specific osteogenic biomarkers into the bloodstream as early precursors to bone formation.

cards.front: Which exercise characteristics and specific loading principles maximize osteogenic stimuli for bone growth?
cards.back: Bone growth is maximized by using multijoint structural exercises (e.g., back squat, power clean, deadlift) that direct heavy axial force vectors through the spine and hip using heavy loads (1- to 10RM). Single-joint machine exercises should be limited, and loading should be varied to alter force vectors across multiple directions.

cards.front: What total repetition volume threshold per session is recommended to optimize new bone formation without diminishing returns?
cards.back: Research indicates that performing a total of 30 to 35 repetitions of heavy structural loading per session provides a maximal osteogenic stimulus. Higher loading volumes do not typically provide any additional adaptive stimulus for bone growth.

cards.front: What is procollagen, and how do fibroblasts process it into active collagen microfibrils?
cards.back: Fibroblasts secrete procollagen, a triple-helix protein strand with protective terminal caps. Extracellular enzymatic cleavage removes these terminal extensions, allowing active collagen molecules to align in parallel into long filaments called microfibrils. Strong chemical covalent cross-linking between collagen molecules provides high tensile strength.

cards.front: How does the vascularity of tendons and ligaments compare to skeletal muscle, and what clinical implication does this have?
cards.back: Tendons and ligaments have significantly lower vascularity and blood flow perfusion during exercise compared to skeletal muscle. Consequently, tendon metabolism is much slower, resulting in prolonged healing and regeneration timelines following connective tissue injury.

cards.front: What specific ultrastructural adaptations occur within tendons to increase load-bearing capacity following high-intensity anaerobic training?
cards.back:
High-intensity anaerobic training enhances tendon tensional capacity through four key adaptations:
  • An increase in collagen fibril diameter
  • A greater number of covalent cross-links within hypertrophied fibers
  • An increase in the total number of collagen fibrils
  • An increase in the packing density of collagen fibrils

cards.front: What magnitude of increase in tendon stiffness occurs following resistance training, and what load intensity is required?
cards.back: Heavy resistance training at 80% of 1RM induces a 15% to 19% increase in Achilles tendon stiffness (force transmission per unit of strain). Light loads (20% of 1RM) do not markedly change collagen content or tendon stiffness.

cards.front: What are the primary functions of hyaline cartilage and fibrous cartilage, and how do chondrocytes receive nutrients?
cards.back: Hyaline (articular) cartilage covers joint surfaces for smooth articulation, while fibrous cartilage withstands compression in intervertebral disks. Cartilage is completely avascular and lacks neural supply; resident chondrocytes depend entirely on passive diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid.

cards.front: How does joint movement maintain cartilage viability, and what occurs during prolonged joint immobilization?
cards.back: Movement creates cyclic pressure changes within the joint capsule, driving nutrient-rich synovial fluid into the cartilage matrix. Immobilization prevents fluid diffusion, causing chondrocyte starvation, matrix resorption, and cartilage atrophy (thinning). Moderate-intensity anaerobic exercise increases articular cartilage thickness.
